newsitem.title: JAPAN: Pakistan govt hopes to issue samurai in early 1997.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan govt hopes to issue samurai in early 1997.

text.p: Pakistan hopes to issue a samurai bond in the early part of 1997 to provide capital for development, adviser to the caretaker government Shahid Javed Burki said.

Burki, who advises Pakistan's caretaker prime minister on financial and economic affaris, told Reuters Financial Television in an interview: "We have had some preliminary discussions with securities agencies and the idea is to come to the Japanese market to tap the yen market."
There was no further information on the bond issue.

In the interview, Burki said there was "no doubt" that Pakistan would receive $160 million under a standby loan with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) immediately after the board meets on December 13.
Early in November, an IMF mission visiting Pakistan agreed to recommend the reactivation of the $600 million standby loan.
The deal would involve the swift release of two tranches of $80 million each to shore up Pakistan's low foreign reserves.
In addition, Burki said he would begin discussions next week on a longer-term IMF lending programme known as an enhanced structural adjustment facility.
Pakistan has also asked the World Bank to provide balance of payments support to reform its financial sector.
"I hope this will come as a single tranche," Burki said. "As to when that will happen, my expectation is that we will be able to do it sometime in January."
The IMF has been concerned about whether accords negotiated with the caretaker government led by Meraj Khalid would be honoured by the new government that takes power after elections on February 3.
Benazir Bhutto, who was sacked on November 5 on disputed corruption charges, has said the caretaker government has no legal right to enter into any long-term agreement with the IMF.
Burki disagreed and said the program Pakistan was working on was one Bhutto's government had initially negotiated.
"These commitments will not be undone by the successor government. The reason is that there is political consensus about the things that we are doing," Burki said.

Burki is on three-months leave from the World Bank to assist the caretaker government until the elections. He was in Japan this week to meet securities firms. He leaves Tokyo on Saturday for New York.
